text: Pulau Bukom is closed to the public, reached by a workers' ferry, and it has been handling oil longer than any other place in Singapore — since 1892, when what its tanks held was not petrol for cars but kerosene for lamps.
It was a storage island first, then a town of five thousand people, then Singapore's first refinery.
Before oil, it was a mangrove island known to passing ships as a place to take on fresh water — the Dutch called it Zoetwater-eiland, Freshwater Island.
It opened on the 16th of September 1892, when the first shipment arrived aboard the S.S. Murex.
As the Japanese advanced down the peninsula, the British torched forty-two of the tanks to keep the oil from falling into enemy hands.
In the early 1960s as many as five thousand people lived on Bukom, most of them Shell employees and their families.

The agreement with the Singapore government was signed on the 1st of March 1960, construction began that June, and on the 26th of July 1961 the Finance Minister, Goh-Keng-Swee, officially opened Singapore's first oil refinery.

As operations spread onto Bukom Kechil, the inhabitants there — some two thousand people — were resettled around 1970 to make way for crude oil storage; where they all went, the record does not say, and the named moves that survive are individual ones, like Madi's family to Kaki Bukit.
On the 31st of January 1974, Bukom became the scene of Singapore's first encounter with international terrorism.
In court, the scheme was put at more than 350,000 tonnes of gas oil, worth over 200 million Singapore dollars — the largest theft of its kind in Singapore.

The island now trades as the Aster Energy and Chemicals Park — a refinery of 237,000 barrels a day, on the sale documents' figures, with its 1.1 million-tonne-a-year cracker — and in September 2026 its new owners launched a terminals business around Bukom's thirteen wharves and tank storage.

At the National Day Rally in August 2026, the Prime Minister announced a long-term plan to merge Pulau Semakau, Pulau Bukom and Pulau Sudong into a new "Western Island", for advanced manufacturing, power generation and defence, linked to Jurong Island — a plan measured in decades, still under study, with marine groups raising attributed concerns for the reefs of the southern islands.
Bukom is the industry's first address, and it has never closed.
